prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms opened a new regime of precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B014 as a single-achievement prize for Katori and Ye. After the first round I think the scientific case can be put in one sentence, which the Chair asked for. At the magic wavelength the light shift of both clock levels is the same, so a lattice can hold thousands of neutral atoms tightly enough that Doppler and recoil shifts vanish (the Lamb-Dicke regime), while the atom number lowers quantum projection noise. The ion clocks honoured in 2012 get their small systematics from a single trapped ion; the comb honoured in 2005 is the ruler that counts optical cycles. The lattice clock is neither: it is a different way of getting both low systematics and high stability, and it works because of one idea. That is why the result has been reproduced independently in several laboratories at the 1e-18 level and has gone on to give new physics (gravitational redshift over millimetres to centimetres, many-body shifts in the lattice, bounds on drifting constants). On the priority history, as I recall it and subject to checking: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock around 2001-2003 and demonstrated the strontium transition in a lattice with Takamoto; Ye's group then brought the strontium clock to record uncertainty. I would want an expert check of the dates before the final citation is fixed. Where colleagues treat my support with caution because I am close to the field, I accept that and have tried to test the case against the best objections rather than rely on the opening ranking.
statement.case_against: The distinctness objection is the real one and I do not think it can be argued away; it can only be answered by a judgement. A colleague who sees one field honoured three times (1989, 2005, 2012) will not be convinced by me, and I will not claim the question is closed. Ion clocks have also reached about 1e-18, so a citation must not suggest that only lattice clocks do. The SI second has not been redefined, so part of the impact is prospective, although I still do not think a scientific prize should wait for an administrative decision. The credited pair leaves out Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others, and Ye's own early training in the comb work that was honoured in 2005 is one more reason to word the citation as invention of the lattice clock and not as credit for the whole field. Finally, Danielsson's objection that a clock measures a world we already knew while IceCube shows us a part we had not seen has force; my answer is that the clock has already shown something new (time dilation over a centimetre), but I accept that this is a matter of weighing.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether I would defend the distinction between the lattice clock and the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes against a colleague who sees one field honoured three times, and he moved B014 to the head of his configuration partly because of the physics argument.
responses.response: Yes, I would defend it, and I would put it this way in committee. The 2005 prize was for the frequency comb, which lets one count optical cycles; the 2012 prize was for control and measurement of individual quantum systems, with ion clocks as an application. Neither tells you how to interrogate many neutral atoms at once without Doppler, recoil or light shifts spoiling the line. The magic wavelength does that, and without it a lattice clock does not exist. That is a single idea with a single originator, not a continuation of either earlier prize. I still accept that someone who counts by field and not by idea will disagree, and I do not want you to read your own move as settled by my argument alone. I would also note, as you do, that the priority dates are from my memory and should be checked.

responses.point: Olsson asks me, as the member closest to the field, to check the 2001-2003 dates for the magic-wavelength proposal and for the first strontium lattice demonstration before the citation is fixed, and says her acceptance of a two-name credit depends on Katori's priority holding.
responses.response: That is the right condition and I will state what I recall and what I cannot confirm. Katori's proposal of the magic-wavelength trap came in 2001-2003, with the engineered light-shift trap paper with Takamoto and Ovsiannikov in 2003; the first resolved 1S0-3P0 spectroscopy of strontium in a lattice followed from his group and then a clock-quality demonstration. Ye's group and the Paris and Boulder groups did early strontium and mercury work in parallel and then drove the uncertainty down, with Ye's record from the late 2000s through 2015-2019. I have not checked these against the papers here, so I ask that we obtain an expert historical note before the final ballot. If Katori's priority holds, I think the structure of the credit is sound: invention for Katori, realisation at record performance for Ye. Takamoto, who co-authored the first demonstrations, is the name I find hardest to leave out, and I would not object to a note in the citation that is explicit about the scope.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B014 fifth because he weighs a measuring invention below a discovery from nature, says the clock measures a world we already knew while IceCube shows a part we had not seen, and states that B014 is his first alternative.
responses.response: I take the distinction seriously, because I made it myself in my opening ranking when I wrote that discoveries are what move me. But I would not call the lattice clock only a better measurement. It gave the first laboratory test of time dilation across millimetre heights, it exposed many-body interaction shifts in a lattice, and it sets limits on drifting constants and on some dark-matter couplings. Those are statements about nature. On IceCube I maintain the point that source identification is still thin, but you are right that the discovery being claimed is the flux, not a source catalogue, and I no longer think maturity is my best objection. Mine is attribution: three names from a collaboration of hundreds plus the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA lineage, and I defer to you and Pearce on that, not on the physics. If the committee wanted to reconsider B021, it would need an expert note on independent confirmation and on credit before I would be comfortable with it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B016, notes that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp form the best-defined theory-plus-experiment core, argues that a prize need not exhaust a field, and asks whether the clock is an enabling instrument or a discovery.
responses.response: Your argument that a prize can name a core without claiming the whole field has moved me a little: I will place B016 first among my alternatives, above B008 and B020. But I do not think the credit gap is the same size in the two cases. For the clock the omitted contributors added pieces to an invention that has one originator; for B016 the missing names include the proposers of the very system in which the effect was seen, and one of them is deceased, so the gap cannot be repaired by a later year. On instrument versus discovery, I would say the lattice clock is an instrument in the sense that a laser or an ion trap is: its value is that it showed us something we could not observe before. You are better placed than I am to judge the condensed-matter side, and I would defer to you on the weight of the 2016 prize.

responses.point: Kroll agrees on the Lamb-Dicke argument, keeps B008 as his first alternative and says that B020 should wait because the three-person limit forces an indefensible choice among Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee.
responses.response: I accept your argument on B020. I listed the Higgs experiments as an alternative in round 1 because the discovery is beyond question, but I cannot offer a defensible three-name cut either, and I have therefore removed it from my alternatives. On B008 I stay where I was: Wineland's 2012 prize covers a large part of the ion-gate foundation, and the compound credit forces a split between the neutral-atom and ion communities that I cannot defend. We agree the question for the final ballot is which single-achievement prize survives scrutiny, and that the clock does so on both the science and the attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; this is a judgement, and I cannot make it certain.

The exact priority dates for Katori's proposal and the first lattice demonstrations, and the position of Takamoto, Lemonde and Lisdat, which I have not checked against the papers and which an expert note should settle before the final citation.
Whether a citation can be worded so that it does not imply that only neutral-atom lattice clocks reach 1e-18, since ion clocks have also done so.
Whether the redefinition of the SI second should be awaited; I think not, but I accept that others weigh it differently.

How much of my own and the committee's support for B014 is a result of members moving toward it, as the Chair notes; I have tried to rest my preference on the science and attribution and not on the count.
statement.conflict_note: No documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. My many-body atomic theory work is close to the clock community, and I flag this proximity again so that colleagues can discount my support for B014 as they see fit. My long-standing collaboration with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups concerns a different field and no candidate on the shortlist. I do not think recusal is needed for B014, but I would accept the committee's view if it disagrees.
